drills.label: Cold open
drills.question_line: SAM: Multi-agent research system. A user asks, "What year did the E U A I Act enter into force?"
drills.answer_line: SAM: A. That is the guide's skill bullet almost word for word
drills.stem: Asked "What year did the EU AI Act enter into force?", the coordinator sends it to all four subagents and returns a 12-page cited report three minutes later. It does this for every question, simple or broad. Which change fixes this best?

options.A: Coordinator analyses what each query needs and invokes only the subagents it calls for
options.B: A rule that sends any query under 15 words down a short path
options.C: Cap every subagent at a small number of turns so the full run finishes faster
options.D: Tell the report subagent to keep reports short when the question is simple

drills.why: Coordinators analyse query requirements and select which subagents to invoke. Word count is a poor proxy for complexity; D treats the symptom at the wrong layer.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Multi-agent research system. Reports on contested topics come back with citations missing
drills.answer_line: SAM: A and B. A gives synthesis the material
drills.stem: Choose two. Reports on contested topics lack citations, and twice gave one market-size figure where two sources disagreed. The coordinator spawns synthesis with a one-paragraph prose summary of what search and analysis found.

options.A: Include the complete search and analysis findings directly in the synthesis subagent's prompt
options.B: Pass each finding as a structured record: claim, evidence excerpt, source URL or document, page number
options.C: Spawn synthesis inside the coordinator's session so it inherits earlier findings automatically
options.D: Add "always cite your sources" to the synthesis subagent's system prompt
options.E: Pass the full raw text of every page the search subagent retrieved

drills.why: A gives synthesis the material; B keeps each claim tied to its source. Subagents do not inherit parent context (C); D asks for citations it never got.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Developer productivity. Your agent uses an explore subagent to map an unfamiliar legacy service
drills.answer_line: ALEX: A. Take the tool away and it cannot write.
drills.stem: An explore subagent maps a legacy service before engineers change it. Twice this week it edited files while "tidying", and one edit broke a build. The system prompt already says read only. What is the best change?

options.A: Restrict the explore subagent's definition to the Read, Grep and Glob tools
options.B: Rewrite the system prompt in capitals and add an example of a read-only run
options.C: Log every file write so engineers can review and revert changes
options.D: Remove Task from the coordinator's allowed tools so no subagent runs unsupervised

drills.why: Removing the tool removes the capability at the root. B is probabilistic and already failed; C is a detective control; D throws away the whole design.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Multi-agent research system. A user asks how European hospitals are adopting A I.
drills.answer_line: SAM: That's miss pattern one, real-world instinct overriding the guide
drills.stem: Asked how European hospitals are adopting AI, synthesis covers imaging and scheduling well but has almost nothing on nursing workflows or procurement, both named in the request. Which design closes gaps like this best?

options.A: Coordinator checks output against the request, re-queries missing areas, re-runs synthesis until coverage
options.B: Run the whole pipeline three times on every request and merge the three reports
options.C: Instruct synthesis to fill thin areas from its own knowledge so the report is complete
options.D: Let synthesis call the web search subagent directly whenever it spots a gap

drills.why: Gap closing is the coordinator's loop, stopping on coverage. D breaks hub-and-spoke; B is a fixed iteration count; C invents uncited claims.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Developer productivity. An engineer asks your agent to review a twenty-two-file branch
drills.answer_line: SAM: A. Per-file passes fix the uneven depth
drills.stem: Reviewing a 22-file branch, the agent is thorough on the first few files, shallow on the rest, and missed that a renamed field in one module broke two callers elsewhere. What is the best change?

options.A: A local analysis pass on each file, then a separate cross-file integration pass
options.B: Move to a model with a larger context window so all 22 files fit comfortably
options.C: Add "review every file with equal care and check cross-file effects" to the prompt
options.D: Spawn one subagent per file and merge their findings as the final review

drills.why: Per-file passes fix uneven depth; the integration pass catches broken callers. B is scale over structure; D is half right, with no integration pass.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Developer productivity. An engineer asks the agent to find out why a legacy billing export
drills.answer_line: SAM: B. Intermittent, unknown code, root cause not yet known
drills.stem: Find out why a legacy billing export sometimes drops records overnight. Nobody on the team knows the code. Which decomposition fits?

options.A: Fixed five-step pipeline: export script, scheduler config, database schema, logs, report
options.B: Map structure with Grep and Glob, form hypotheses, create next subtasks from each finding, reprioritise
options.C: Spawn one subagent per file in the repository in parallel and merge what they report
options.D: Read every file first and only then decide what to investigate

drills.why: Intermittent, unknown code, unknown cause: open-ended investigation, so dynamic decomposition. A fixes steps before learning; D is the exhaustive-survey trap.

drills.question_line: SAM: Before the next episode, recall. Pause and name the five segments, and the giveaway for each.
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Hub-and-spoke. Isolated context. Spawning with Task.
drills.prompt: Name the five segments, and the giveaway for each.
drills.answer: Hub-and-spoke. Isolated context. Spawning with Task. Coverage: duplication and gaps. A fixed pipeline against dynamic decomposition.
